g1.title: The Cardboard on the Kitchen Door
g1.where: An alley in a seaside city, the Philippines
g1.obj: A piece of cardboard with the family's values
g1.age: Read together from age 6 · about 12 minutes
g1.label: The characters, the place and every event were made up by the writer, based on the content of the course. The story is not modelled on any real family.
bullets: What it does
keeps the four things the whole family chose together, where everyone can see them.
Who gets to look at it
the children and the parents. Grown-ups get reminded too.
In our home
a sheet of paper, a pen and a fifteen-minute meeting each week are enough.
qs: Why did Mother mean to leave the hundred-peso note until "tomorrow"? What changed her mind?
Bea did not say a word, and her mother still understood. Why?
How is our family like Bea's? If we wrote it down, what would our family treasure most?
g1.act: When Sunday dinner is over, our family will meet for fifteen minutes and write down three to five things we value.
safe: A family meeting is a time to listen to one another, not a time to list faults.
House rules are clear and consistent, with no hitting or shouting.
Young children use pens and scissors with a grown-up sitting beside them.
g1.more: The course "Our family values": choose 3–5 values, turn them into actions, set clear house rules, hold a family meeting every week.

g2.title: The Toy Bag on Tuesdays
g2.where: A poor neighbourhood in Kingston, Jamaica
g2.age: For the whole family, from age 6 · about 12 minutes
g2.label: In 1986–1989 in Kingston, community health workers visited homes for one hour a week over two years, bringing home-made toys and showing mothers how to play and talk with their young children. Twenty years later, the children who had been visited were earning about 25% more on average. Marva, Devon, Miss Pearl and all the dialogue are composite characters created by the writer.
bullets: What it does
it rattles, so the baby looks, reaches and "asks" the grown-up something.
What it is made of
a clean plastic bottle, a few large caps, and a lid screwed on very tightly.
What matters more than the bottle
a grown-up who sits down and answers the child, a little every day.
qs: At first, what did Marva think about talking to a baby who could not talk yet?
Why did Miss Pearl praise the mother before she praised the baby?
How is our family like Marva's? What did the baby in our home "ask" today?
g2.act: When the child looks, points or babbles, our family will stop, look where the child is looking, and answer with a short sentence.
safe: Toys for children under 3: no small parts; lids screwed tight and sealed.
Never leave a baby alone with a bottle that has small objects inside.
Worried that a child is slow to talk or grow: see a health worker; do not wait.
g2.more: The course "Family 0–2": the five steps of serve and return, reading from early on, safe sleep, a plan for when the baby cries.

g3.title: The Yellow Can That Takes a Bow
g3.where: A town near Lake Volta, eastern Ghana
g3.obj: A handwashing tap made from a plastic can
g3.age: Read together from age 4 · about 12 minutes
g3.label: A seven-year-old girl saw a handwashing station at school, went home and kept asking until her family had one, and became the youngest handwashing monitor in her school. Names have been changed. The dialogue, the grandmother and many details were added by the writer.
bullets: What it does
a foot presses the stick, the can tips, water runs. Dirty hands never touch the can.
What you need
a clean plastic can, two posts, a crossbar, string and soap.
If your home has a tap
no can needed. Only soap, and remembering to wash before eating and after the toilet.
qs: Dzifa's family already had a basin. Why did she still want a tap made from a can?
What did Grandmother say to Father? Why do you think Father changed his mind?
How is our family like Dzifa's? Is there something our family keeps leaving "for tomorrow"?
g3.act: When the family is about to sit down to dinner, we will wash our hands with soap under running water. The child is the one who reminds us.
safe: Anything with knives, nails or fire is a job for grown-ups.
The water in the can is only for washing hands, not for drinking.
Young children wash their hands with a grown-up standing by.
g3.more: The course "Family 2–8": I can do it myself, hands-on science, honesty, gratitude, kindness, responsibility.

g4.title: The One-Letter Message
g4.where: A town in the hill country of the eastern United States
g4.age: For the whole family, from age 10 · about 12 minutes
g4.label: In 2017 a father in the United States who works with teenagers described what his family does: the child texts the letter X, a family member calls back to say something has come up and comes to collect them, with no questions asked; the only exception is when someone else is still in danger. Caleb, his family and the evening in the story were created by the writer.
bullets: What it does
gives a child a reason to leave without losing face in front of friends.
What makes it work
the promise of no questions on the way home, and parents who keep that promise.
The exception
if anyone there is still in danger, the child must say so.
qs: Why did Caleb find it hard to stand up, even though he knew he should go home?
In the truck, Father asked only two questions. Why do you think he asked no more?
How is our family like Caleb's? What code would our family like to choose?
g4.act: When the child texts the code, the parents will call back at once, come to collect them, and ask no questions on the way home.
safe: A code does not replace parents knowing where their child is going, and with whom.
In Vietnam: immediate danger, call 113; a child needs help, call 111. Elsewhere, use your local emergency number.
Parents driving to collect a child: stay calm, and never text while driving.
g4.more: The course "Families with children 10–14": fifteen minutes alone with your child, listening, family agreements, practising how to say no.

g5.title: The Teapot at Nine O'Clock
g5.where: A port city in western Türkiye
g5.age: For the whole family, from age 8 · about 12 minutes
g5.label: The characters, the place and every event were made up by the writer, based on the content of the course. The story is not modelled on any real family.
bullets: What it does
keeps a fixed hour for grown-ups to talk about hard things, once the child is asleep.
Three things that go with it
no arguing in front of the child; begin with a thank-you; speak with one voice in front of the child.
If your home does not drink tea
a glass of water, an agreed hour and two words to remind each other are enough.
qs: What did Defne's first drawing tell her parents?
Why did Defne not cry when Father said the same as Mother?
How is our family like Defne's? When the grown-ups disagree, how does it feel to you?
g5.act: When one person's voice begins to rise, the two of us will say "tonight", then go on with the talk after the child is asleep, opening with a thank-you.
safe: This story and this course are not meant for relationships where there is violence.
If you are being hit, threatened or controlled: safety comes first. In Vietnam, call 113 in danger and 117 about domestic violence. Elsewhere, use your local emergency number.
In Vietnam, if a child is being harmed, call 111.
g5.more: The course "Parents as one team": appreciating each other, talking when you disagree, keeping children out of arguments.
